{"id": "41:39/q05", "question": "Why portray barren earth as humbled?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording is a borrowed quality, an implied comparison of the entire transformation, or an ethical image.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q05/p1", "position": "Humility is borrowed metaphorically for the land’s low, bare, diminished appearance.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī identify the borrowing from submission. Ibn ʿAṭiyya likens drought-struck earth to a downcast person almost weeping; Biqāʿī likens it to a powerless flattened person; Bursevī to an overlooked lowly person. Ibn ʿĀshūr treats humbled and shook as mapped parts of one personifying metaphor."}, {"id": "41:39/q05/p2", "position": "The whole scene is a representative comparison: a shabby, neglected person becomes lively and proud after receiving adornment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers the implied whole-scene comparison, its humbling and swaying standing in for the omitted comparison. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares a poor person transformed by wealth into a splendid figure. Ibn ʿĀshūr maps the earth’s initial abasement and later shoulder-shaking to a person."}, {"id": "41:39/q05/p3", "position": "The humble image warns the arrogant and anticipates the humble person’s rise.", "reasons": "Elmalılı describes earth as a bowed-neck person and explicitly draws both lessons."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q06", "question": "Why does this verse say “humbled” here and stop before describing sprouting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q06/p1", "position": "The wording fits the surrounding scene of worship; explicit sprouting and emergence would not fit it.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says this depiction resembles a worshipper more closely than al-Ḥajj 22:5. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the worship setting at 41:37 with 22:5 and explains the stopping point."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q07", "question": "What is the water sent down onto the earth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q07/p1", "position": "It is rain.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī identify it as rain. Al-Ṭabarī specifies rain from the sky. Biqāʿī adds that rain may come from clouds or be driven from high places and carry growth-suitable soil even to saline land such as Egypt."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q08", "question": "Why does the wording switch to “We sent down”?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q08/p1", "position": "The majestic plural marks power and greatness while stressing that sending rain belongs to God alone.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī treats the rainfall as one of the strongest signs of the One."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q09", "question": "How does the earth “shake” after rain?", "turns_on": "Whether the observed movement belongs primarily to plants, to the loosened soil, or to a personified expression of joy.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q09/p1", "position": "It stirs as vegetation emerges or moves across it.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Mujāhid, al-Kalbī and others explain it by sprouting or moving growth; al-Qurṭubī adds that ihtazz denotes movement and cites a poet’s quivering sword-blade image. Biqāʿī intensifies the motion as great, abundant and quick, as if self-initiated; Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī locate the movement in the plants."}, {"id": "41:39/q09/p2", "position": "Water loosens the soil and makes it crack open for plants.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains the movement as the earth’s parts loosening and splitting."}, {"id": "41:39/q09/p3", "position": "The shaking figuratively expresses the earth’s joy at rain.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the comparison with the earth’s splitting for plants being called laughter."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q10", "question": "What does “it swelled” describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the increase describes the soil’s physical elevation or the amount and growth of its vegetation.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q10/p1", "position": "The wetted soil expands, rises and often splits before plants emerge.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says swelled and reports al-Suddī’s expanded; Qatāda observes rain in the surface swelling; Mujāhid says it rises before shoots. Al-Zajjāj distinguishes unhamzated rabat as growing or swelling; Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes swelling with water and rising surface. Al-Qurṭubī cites rabwa and rābiya for raised ground; al-Rāzī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr add lifting and cracking. Bursevī cites al-Rāghib’s nurturing-to-grow gloss and the swelling of a horse after exertion or fear. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives growth, flourishing and rising."}, {"id": "41:39/q10/p2", "position": "It increases its vegetation or abundant crop yield.", "reasons": "Muqātil speaks of increased plants. Al-Kalbī links rising to abundant yield; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the plants growing upward. Al-Zajjāj gives growth as the unhamzated sense."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q11", "question": "How are the shaking, swelling and emergence ordered?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbs follow actual time, reverse a swelling-before-sprouting sequence, or describe one state.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q11/p1", "position": "The soil rises first, then vegetation emerges and moves, so the wording may state the events out of temporal order.", "reasons": "Mujāhid places rising before sprouts, and al-Māwardī explicitly reverses the wording to “rose, then moved.” Al-Qurṭubī reports this sequence as rabat then ihtazzat."}, {"id": "41:39/q11/p2", "position": "The shaking and swelling may occur before or after shoots; vegetation first moves outward and then expands in several directions.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports either timing, with growth raising soil and later growth increasing height, length and width."}, {"id": "41:39/q11/p3", "position": "Shaking and swelling name a single state of vegetation emerging.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this additional view."}, {"id": "41:39/q11/p4", "position": "After rain the earth moves, swells, then splits to bring out plants.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī gives this explicit sequence; Biqāʿī describes cracking, surface-covering growth, roots branching and stems thickening until passage becomes hard."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q12", "question": "How is وَرَبَتْ read?", "turns_on": "Presence of a hamza after bāʾ and the associated nuance of elevated ground versus swelling or increase.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q12/p1", "position": "The majority read rabat without hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the reading to the majority; Ibn al-Jazarī says other readers omit Abū Jaʿfar’s added hamza."}, {"id": "41:39/q12/p2", "position": "A variant reads rabaʾat with a hamza after bāʾ, meaning rose or increased.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj gives the variant and contrasts its rising sense with rabat’s swelling. Al-Naḥḥās derives it from a lookout rising to a high place. Ibn ʿAṭiyya names Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ and al-Ruʾāsī from Abū ʿAmr; al-Qurṭubī names Abū Jaʿfar and Khālid. Ibn al-Jazarī names Abū Jaʿfar in this verse and al-Ḥajj; Ibn ʿĀshūr and the qirāʾāt note likewise name him. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī gloss the variant as rose or increased, with al-Ālūsī transmitting al-Zajjāj’s distinction."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q13", "question": "What is the derivation and dual of ربت?", "turns_on": "The root and orthography implied by the Qurʾanic form and whether the dual follows the Basran or Kufan analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q13/p1", "position": "It derives from rabā yarbū and its dual is rabawān.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports Sībawayh’s derivation and says Abū Jaʿfar prefers this Basran analysis because the Qurʾanic form supports it; he cites 30:39. Abū Isḥāq rebukes the Kufans for extending an orthographic mistake to the dual."}, {"id": "41:39/q13/p2", "position": "Its dual is rabiyān and rabā is written with yāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports the Kufan account; Abū Jaʿfar and Abū Isḥāq reject its spelling basis."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q14", "question": "In what sense is the earth revived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q14/p1", "position": "Its life is a figure for greenness, renewed freshness, flowering and seeds sprouting; God is literally the one who causes this revival.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir distinguishes figurative earthly life from the literal attribution of revival to God. Bursevī calls it the stirring of growth powers and the renewal of freshness by varied plants. Ibn ʿĀshūr says rain makes buried seeds sprout and the relative subject explains why God is called the reviver."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q15", "question": "What does reviving the earth establish about the dead?", "turns_on": "Whether the contextual force of the analogy is bodily resurrection or the possible awakening of closed hearts.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q15/p1", "position": "God can and will raise dead human bodies after death, as rain revives barren ground.", "reasons": "Muqātil addresses doubters; al-Ṭabarī says even decayed bodies can be restored; al-Māwardī calls observable earth evidence for deniers, moving from visible to unseen. Al-Rāzī says scattered parts can be reassembled and life, intellect and ability restored because all possibles are within power. Biqāʿī adds that plant remains decay into soil just as bodies do. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the likeness persuasive rather than demonstrative, fitting deniers’ appeal to customary improbability; the closing power claim strengthens it. Al-Qurṭubī links 22:5 and Study Quran lists 7:57, 16:65, 22:5, 25:48–89, 29:63, 30:19, 30:24, 30:50, 35:9, 36:33, 43:11, 45:5 and 50:9–11."}, {"id": "41:39/q15/p2", "position": "Here the earth’s revival especially illustrates God’s power to give spiritual life to closed hearts.", "reasons": "Asad acknowledges the common bodily-resurrection symbolism but reads this context of 41:33–39 as a promise of spiritual awakening; it encourages hope that deniers may understand the Qurʾan. Kur’an Yolu says the absolute life-giving power can also encompass enlightenment and mental clarity."}]}

{"id": "41:39/q19", "question": "What is included in God’s power over every thing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q19/p1", "position": "His power covers all things He wills, including life, death and resurrection; no intended act escapes Him.", "reasons": "Muqātil names resurrection and all else; al-Ṭabarī says no intention defeats or eludes Him. {"id": "41:39/q21", "question": "How can the earthly revival be read as a change in hearts?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward “rain” is mercy and knowledge yielding repentance or trial that activates latent sin.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q21/p1", "position": "Awareness of sin humbles hearts, and divine mercy makes them flourish in regret, repentance and forgiveness.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī compares parched winter earth with hearts made humble by sin-awareness, then turned to by God. {"id": "41:39/q22", "question": "How does the verse relate to the surrounding discourse and other revival passages?", "turns_on": "The notes give both an immediate contextual sequence and intertextual parallels, which are complementary.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q22/p1", "position": "It moves from heavenly signs to an earthly sign within an argument for exclusive divinity that also makes room for resurrection.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī contrasts Yāsīn 36:33, where resurrection and earth’s proof are more prominent. He says the sun and moon’s unspecified motions leave all their conditions as evidence, while their creation recalls the heavens. Islahi sees proofs of oneness and Hereafter followed by censure of opposition. {"id": "41:39/q25", "question": "How do distant comparisons and novel figurative predications create rhetorical force?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison merely recalls a familiar object or establishes an unfamiliar image with its own novel properties.", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q25/p1", "position": "A likeness between distant kinds is more surprising and pleasing than a familiar likeness.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir contrasts eye and narcissus with the more particular Pleiades as grape cluster, silver bridle or necklace; a cited poem’s blue violet resembles early flames on sulfur tips among red gems, stronger than narcissus as jeweled bowls. The unfamiliar setting gives delight that a same-kind flower or ordinary colored object would lack."}, {"id": "41:39/q25/p2", "position": "A novel metaphor can posit a new kind of subject, whose unusual property cannot be conveyed by ordinary simile markers.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir says al-Buḥturī makes a praised man an established, new moon-like being that leaves one spot dark. Kāf, kaʾanna, taḥsab and takhāl instead suggest uncertainty about an understood predicate or familiar metaphor; here the phenomenon itself is new."}, {"id": "41:39/q25/p3", "position": "A plain comparison to the familiar moon would make that moon illuminate the earth but leave the speaker’s saddle dark.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir rejects this reading of al-Buḥturī’s poem as absurd."}]}
{"id": "41:39/q26", "question": "How do composition and neighboring meanings affect rhetorical excellence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:39/q26/p1", "position": "Force and beauty arise from words arranged to express a meaning; grammatical relations, placement and context determine their effect.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir says merit lies in the expressed form, not sounds alone; an image of ravines flowing toward a person loses sweetness if its adverbials move. He says adding an object changes a transitive verb’s asserted meaning, illustrating with a proverb and in atāka Zayd atāka li-ḥāja. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports his view that grammar belongs in the discourse’s order and that a word’s excellence depends on fit with neighbors, as one word can please in one place and feel heavy in another."}]}

{"id": "42:13/q04", "question": "What is the force of min in “of the religion”?", "turns_on": "Redundant versus partitive.", "positions": [{"id": "42:13/q04/p1", "position": "Min is extra: the phrase means “the religion.”", "reasons": "Muqatil, Mawardi and Damghani gloss it away; Damghani compares 24:30 and 12:101."}, {"id": "42:13/q04/p2", "position": "Min is partitive and al-din generically covers earlier revealed religions.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur's grammatical account."}]}
{"id": "42:13/q05", "question": "What common religion did the prophets receive?", "turns_on": "The boundary between unchanging fundamentals, shared rules, and all binding revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "42:13/q05/p1", "position": "One Islam of monotheism, obedience, basic beliefs, ethics and some shared practice.", "reasons": "Mujahid says every prophet carried one religion. {"id": "42:13/q08", "question": "Why al-ladhī for Muhammad and mā for prior prophets?", "turns_on": "A known versus generally known law, or avoidance of repetition.", "positions": [{"id": "42:13/q08/p1", "position": "Al-ladhī marks a known, detailed law; mā suits earlier laws known only generally.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains the relative forms through 4:58, 50:23 and poetry; Samarrai agrees."}, {"id": "42:13/q08/p2", "position": "Variation avoids repeating the same relative form three times.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur mentions but prefers the semantic distinction."}]}
